First-timer field guide · 12 min read

Your first trip to Japan is not a checklist. Do these five things first.

Tokyo, Kyoto and Mount Fuji may shape the itinerary. Five smaller choices shape the experience: how you move, what you carry, how you enter, where you eat and whether you let Japan slow you down.

Researched and edited in Japan by Yuji Shimizu · Published October 10, 2026

A first journey to Japan is unusually easy to over-plan. A map fills with red gates, ramen counters, observation decks and day trips until every hour becomes a transfer. You arrive with a perfect list and spend the week looking at a clock.

The better first trip begins with a paradox: do fewer headline things, but learn how Japan works. The country becomes more legible once you tap through a ticket gate without stopping, send a suitcase ahead, recognize a shrine before reaching the altar, order lunch at a tiny counter and understand why a bath asks you to wash before entering clean water.

The real first-timer advantage: Japan rewards fluency in small systems more than heroic scheduling. Learn five of them early and the rest of the trip becomes calmer, kinder and more spontaneous.

1. Get an IC card—then ride one stop beyond the plan

A Suica, PASMO or another interoperable IC card is stored value, not an unlimited rail pass. Touch in, touch out, and the fare is calculated. It works across much of the national train and bus network and at many convenience stores, vending machines and lockers.

Buy or set up the version that suits your phone and arrival point, then keep yen as backup. Tourist cards can have different sales locations, validity and refund rules. An IC card also does not replace every reserved-seat, limited-express or Shinkansen ticket. Check the operator when the train is faster or more special than an ordinary local service.

The cultural benefit is not the card itself. It removes friction, which gives you permission to get off one station early, follow a shopping street, or choose a neighborhood because the light looks good. Do not stop immediately past a gate, and keep conversations quiet on crowded trains.

2. Send the large suitcase ahead

Japan’s rail system feels effortless until a roller bag meets a busy platform, staircase or Kyoto bus. The takuhaibin courier network offers a more revealing solution: luggage can move between airports, hotels and service counters while you take the train with an overnight bag.

JNTO’s Hands-Free Travel guidance notes that major airports and many hotels support delivery or storage. Size, weight, contents and timing limits apply, and same-day delivery is not universal. Ask when the bag will arrive, keep medicine and the next day’s essentials with you, and check the carrier’s terms.

Traveling light changes behavior. You can use a local bus without occupying the aisle, walk from the station through an old district, or insert a one-night ryokan stay between city hotels. On some Shinkansen routes, oversized baggage requires a designated seat reservation, making advance planning important.

3. Visit one shrine and one temple slowly

A torii gate generally announces a Shinto shrine; a Buddhist temple often has a sanmon gate and images of Buddhas or bodhisattvas. Japan’s religious history is more intertwined than those labels suggest, but noticing the distinction turns architecture into meaning.

At a shrine, bow lightly before the torii, move respectfully, purify at the water basin if it is in use, and follow the local worship pattern. The familiar form is two bows, two claps, a silent prayer and one final bow, but signs and local custom take priority. At a Buddhist temple, do not clap: place your hands together quietly.

The point is not to perform perfectly. Watch what worshippers do, lower your voice, keep out of restricted spaces and ask before photographing people. One unhurried visit teaches more than six rushed gates.

4. Eat at three scales

“Eat sushi and ramen” is not bad advice; it is simply too broad. Start with a convenience-store breakfast or train snack, but look past novelty packaging: compare regional items, seasonal fillings and the precision of everyday service.

At lunch, visit a neighborhood shotengai, a public market that welcomes visitors, or a department-store depachika. These reveal prepared foods, pickles, sweets and gifts without requiring an elaborate order. Respect sampling and photography rules, do not block traffic, and remember that famous markets are workplaces.

Then choose a small counter restaurant. Go before the peak and learn sumimasen, onegaishimasu and gochisōsama deshita. Some shops use ticket machines; some take only cash; some cannot accommodate every allergy in a tiny kitchen. Ask clearly. Do not turn one meal into a marathon queue because social media declared it essential.

5. Try an onsen or sento

An onsen uses naturally hot spring water; a sento is a public bath generally using heated tap water. Remove clothing in the changing area, wash thoroughly at the shower station, rinse away soap, keep hair and the small towel out of the bath, and leave the phone behind.

For many visitors, shared nudity is the obstacle. A private reservable bath can be an alternative. Tattoo rules vary: some facilities welcome tattoos, some allow covers, and others refuse entry. Check the individual policy before arrival. Avoid bathing after alcohol and leave the water if you feel overheated.

A Japanese bath asks you to do nothing. After days built around arrival times and photographs, sitting quietly in hot water restores scale to the journey. The memory may outlast the landmark you rushed to before it.

Before you arrive: leave one thing unbooked

Reserve the scarce pieces—your first nights, a timed museum, a restaurant that truly matters—but do not schedule every meal and neighborhood. Weather changes. Jet lag changes. A place that looked minor online may deserve the afternoon. Blank space is not wasted time; it is the part of the itinerary that can respond to the Japan you actually find.

Also download offline maps, save accommodation names in Japanese, confirm mobile data, and carry a small amount of cash. Cards are widely useful, but a neighborhood shop, temple admission box or rural bus may still require yen. Keep a compact rubbish bag too: public bins can be scarce, and carrying your own waste is normal. These preparations are deliberately boring. That is why they work—they keep logistics from becoming the main memory.

The five are a sequence, not a bucket list

Move easily. Remove the bag. Enter with attention. Eat at human scale. Stop in the bath. Together they make room for surprise and reduce the behaviors that make popular destinations harder for residents: blocked gates, suitcases on buses, sacred spaces used as photo sets, and queues treated as proof of quality.

The goal of a first trip is not to finish Japan. It is to learn how to begin.

Operational details were checked on October 10, 2026. Card availability, transport rules, delivery limits, access and tattoo policies change; confirm official operator information shortly before use.
